560.statement: The battery produces a fixed sized current that splits between each branch of a parallel circuit.
560.correction: Consider each branch of a parallel circuit as a separate series circuit connected to an identical battery, in which the total current through the battery is determined by the current it can push through each of the branches added together.

6367.belief: Most pupils do not discriminate sufficiently between current, voltage, energy and power.
6367.statement: Most pupils do not discriminate sufficiently between current, voltage, energy and power.
6367.correction: Provide pupils with opportunities to calculate energy usage with appliances that have different power ratings and are used for different lengths of time.

6242.statement: Pupils confuse the mass or weight of an object with density.
6242.correction: Provide pupils with a range of objects of varying sizes that they are going to measure the density of. Before measuring density, ask the pupils to rank the objects in order of density with explanations. Compare results to the list after measurements.

5795.belief: The pressure at a particular depth depends on the shape of the container the liquid is in.
5795.statement: The pressure at a particular depth depends on the shape of the container the liquid is in.
5795.correction: Demonstrate different shaped containers with the same depth of water in each and an identical shaped hole 1 cm above the base of each. Identical sized jets of water should shoot out of each hole as the pressure at each hole is (initially) the same.

8497.statement: Pupils often do not understand that even sub–microscopic particles have a mass and volume, which affect the density of a substance.
8497.correction: Use the anomaly of ice floating on water to consolidate understanding that molecules have mass and that the spacing of water molecules can affect density.

6944.statement: Pupils often have the misconception that heat is a substance that can flow.
6944.correction: Focus learning on how heating causes particles to move more quickly, and the effects that this can have on the density of a fluid.

5796.belief: Pressure is a weight or a force; pressure has a preferred downwards direction in a liquid or gas.
5796.statement: Pressure is a weight or a force; pressure has a preferred downwards direction in a liquid or gas.
5796.correction: Use the particle model to provide opportunities for pupils to explain the causes of pressure in a gas that is in a container, and to explain how the difference in pressure between inside and outside causes an outward force.

8524.statement: Pupils often do not have an understanding of what moving at a particular speed means in the real world, and treat answers as ‘just numbers’.
8524.correction: Use real world examples of speeds through examples and questions asked (N.B. 10 m/s is approximately 20 miles per hour).

10439.belief: When the trolley is released, it speeds up quickly at the start and then rolls at a constant speed.
10439.statement: When the trolley is released, it speeds up quickly at the start and then rolls at a constant speed.
10439.correction: Show a video of an accelerating trolley in slow motion identifying the distance travelled in successive equal intervals of time.

3657.belief: It is important for the same person to take all the measurements.
3657.statement: It is important for the same person to take all the measurements.
3657.correction: Emphasise that if the method is a good one then everyone carrying it out carefully should get similar results that show the same pattern (the results are repeatable and reproducible).

7582.statement: Pupils often have a tendency to believe that a velocity must have a positive value and have difficulty in associating a reverse in direction with a change in sign.
7582.correction: It is important to make sure pupils are secure in their knowledge of the vector–scalar distinction; use plenty of visual examples.

4920.belief: Negative values on a displacement-time graph always represent motion that is backwards.
4920.statement: Negative values on a displacement-time graph always represent motion that is backwards.
4920.correction: Provide opportunities for pupils to plot a range of displacement-time graphs in real time in order for them to understand how the graph represents different motions.

5303.belief: A pair of coordinates on a s-t graph can be used to calculate the instantaneous speed or velocity at that point, but that only works for a straight line graph through the origin.
5303.statement: A pair of coordinates on a s-t graph can be used to calculate the instantaneous speed or velocity at that point, but that only works for a straight line graph through the origin.
5303.correction: Ask pupils to calculate the velocity of a graph that represents a steady velocity on a line that does not go through the origin, and to check to see if dividing the values at any point on the line gives the right value for velocity.

8353.belief: If velocity or speed is increasing, then acceleration must also be increasing. Pupils often don't associate a change in direction at a constant speed with an acceleration.
8353.statement: Pupils often think that if velocity or speed is increasing, then acceleration must also be increasing. Pupils often don't associate a change in direction at a constant speed with an acceleration.
8353.correction: Before teaching acceleration, consolidate an understanding of the differences between velocity and changes in velocity. Discuss how an object can be accelerating AND travelling at a constant speed (circular motion).

7839.belief: Final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
7839.statement: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
7839.correction: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.

6202.statement: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
6202.correction: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.

6317.statement: Pupils often consider time in the acceleration equation to be moment in time (perhaps read from a graph) rather than a change in time.
6317.correction: Label the value of t in the acceleration as a change of time rather than just time.

6224.statement: Pupils often confuse displacement–time graphs with velocity–time graphs.
6224.correction: Emphasise the need for pupils to always read the axes of a graph first, before they start to think about any lines drawn on it.

5959.statement: Pupils often apply equations incorrectly or do not spot obvious errors when using them due to not thinking about the science.
5959.correction: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.

4342.belief: Magnetic field effects are often mistaken for electric field effects.
4342.statement: Magnetic field effects are often mistaken for electric field effects.
4342.correction: Be explicit in teaching that electric charges and charged objects are not magnetic.

8575.statement: Pupils often use physics equations without understanding, leading to errors.
8575.correction: Develop a qualitative understanding of potential difference, current and resistance before combining them mathematically. Use the equation as a shorthand for an already understood relationship between them.

7117.statement: Pupils may not realise that the resistance of a wire varies with temperature.
7117.correction: Ensure pupils are aware that the temperature of a metal wire does affect resistance and that precautions should be taken to avoid a temperature change.

9417.belief: To solve circuits you need only to put numbers into equations.
9417.statement: To solve circuits you need only to put numbers into equations.
9417.correction: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.

9416.belief: To solve circuit problems you need only to put numbers into equations.
9416.statement: To solve circuit problems you need only to put numbers into equations.
9416.correction: Talk through circuits with pupils before analysing them in order to develop an intrinsic understanding of how circuits work; research shows this improves pupils’ problem solving ability for electric circuits.

2415.belief: A displacement-distance graph is a picture of a wave, with 1:1 vertical and horizontal scaling.
2415.statement: A displacement-distance graph is a picture of a wave, with 1:1 vertical and horizontal scaling.
2415.correction: Interpret and sketch graphs of waves that are compared to pictures of each wave.

2416.belief: A displacement-time graph is a picture of a wave.
2416.statement: A displacement-time graph is a picture of a wave.
2416.correction: Interpret and sketch displacement-time graphs of waves that are compared to descriptions of each wave.

5333.belief: Particles in a longitudinal wave move forward and backward between one compression and the next.
5333.statement: Particles in a longitudinal wave move forward and backward between one compression and the next.
5333.correction: Demonstrate the movement of a candle flame in front of a loudspeaker set to a very low frequency with a wavelength of about 30 m (at 10 Hz).

2422.belief: The distance between two crests of an oscilloscope graph is equal to one wavelength.
2422.statement: The distance between two crests of an oscilloscope graph is equal to one wavelength.
2422.correction: Emphasise the need to read scales of graphs first and that the horizontal scale of an oscilloscope graph is time.

804.belief: Calculating a mean of repeat readings reduces (random) errors in measurements.
804.statement: Calculating a mean of repeat readings reduces (random) errors in measurements.
804.correction: Calculating a mean reduces the effect that random errors have on a final result. The random errors in the original readings are unaffected.

3174.belief: Frequency or wavelength of waves on a string will affect the wave speed.
3174.statement: Frequency or wavelength of waves on a string will affect the wave speed.
3174.correction: The speed of waves on a string only depends on the properties of the wave medium (the string) e.g. tension, density

10771.belief: In, v = f x λ, speed is dependent on frequency and wavelength, rather than the medium.
10771.statement: In, v = f x λ, speed is dependent on frequency and wavelength, rather than the medium.
10771.correction: Focus on speed being property of a medium and equation not being as an equation with three interdependent variables.

10770.belief: In, v = f × λ, speed is dependent on frequency and wavelength, rather then the medium.
10770.statement: In, v = f × λ, speed is dependent on frequency and wavelength, rather then the medium.
10770.correction: Focus on speed being property of a medium and equation not being as an equation with three interdependent variables.

2716.belief: In the equation for the speed of a wave, v = f x λ, speed is dependent on frequency and/or wavelength.
2716.statement: In the equation for the speed of a wave, v = f x λ, speed is dependent on frequency and/or wavelength.
2716.correction: Emphasise that the speed of a wave depends only on the wave medium and not on frequency or wavelength.

4521.belief: If measurements are repeatable (or precise) then they will also be accurate.
4521.statement: If measurements are repeatable (or precise) then they will also be accurate.
4521.correction: Repeatable (or precise) measurements may involve a systematic error making them inaccurate.

6279.statement: Pupils often confuse the terms force, energy, and work done and use them interchangeably.
6279.correction: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the three terms need to be used appropriately, e.g. in describing energy transfers for pushing (force) a crate (doing work) along a level surface (energy transferred).

6995.statement: Pupils often mix up the terms power and force, which are often used interchangeably in everyday speech.
6995.correction: Provide opportunities for pupils to describe events in which the terms need to be used appropriately, for example in lifting two different sized weights (different forces) whilst increasing their energy at the same rate (same power).

7112.statement: Pupils may not realise that energy transfers usually result in the heating of the surroundings and therefore some energy ends up in a thermal store.
7112.correction: Pupils should have opportunity to identify and describe places in a system where energy is dissipated and transferred into a thermal store.

801.belief: When calculating energy in the kinetic store, pupils often work out ½ mv and then square everything, rather than just the speed.
801.statement: When calculating energy in the kinetic store, pupils often work out ½ mv and then square everything, rather than just the speed.
801.correction: Scaffold calculations to show how kinetic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

7613.belief: The amount of energy in the gravitational store depends on the path taken by an object to change its height, or the speed of an object at a particular height.
7613.statement: Pupils often think that the amount of energy in the gravitational store depends on the path taken by an object to change its height, or the speed of an object at a particular height.
7613.correction: Teaching should include examples of objects increasing height by the same amount by different routes, and examples of objects at the same height moving at different speeds.

2663.belief: Energy can be lost or created in physical processes.
2663.statement: Energy can be lost or created in physical processes.
2663.correction: Always discuss how energy is dissipated to the surroundings when discussing energy transformations, even when dealing with ‘ideal situations’ in which there is no dissipation.

2874.belief: Extension is the extra amount the spring has stretched when a bigger force is applied.
2874.statement: Extension is the extra amount the spring has stretched when a bigger force is applied.
2874.correction: Ensure pupils fully remove each hanging mass between measurements so they see the extension of the spring from its original length each time.

7664.belief: The bigger the spring constant, the more a spring stretches for a given force.
7664.statement: Pupils often think the bigger the spring constant, the more a spring stretches for a given force.
7664.correction: Provide opportunities for pupils to apply understanding that the spring constant describes the stiffness of a spring. The bigger the spring constant, the harder it is to stretch (or compress) the spring.

800.belief: When calculating energy in the elastic store, pupils often work out (½ times spring constant tmes extension) and then square everything, rather than just the extension.
800.statement: When calculating energy in the elastic store, pupils often work out (½ times spring constant tmes extension) and then square everything, rather than just the extension.
800.correction: Scaffold calculations to show how elastic energy is calculated, taking pupils through how to do this on their calculators without making a mistake.

5940.statement: Pupils often do not accept that all objects left in a room for a long time are the same temperature.
5940.correction: Provide opportunities to consolidate the understanding that particles vibrating with more energy transfer some of that energy to particles with less energy through collisions and when bonded together in a solid.

3471.belief: Heat is a substance that flows through an insulator.
3471.statement: Heat is a substance that flows through an insulator.
3471.correction: Always refer to it being particle vibrations that are passed on through a material and do not refer to heat moving.

6238.statement: Pupils confuse ideas about temperature and energy.
6238.correction: Use examples in different contexts to develop and consolidate ideas about differences between temperature and energy.

10153.belief: Often, after teaching, pupils often do not understand what specific heat capacity means.
10153.statement: Often, after teaching, pupils often do not understand what specific heat capacity means.
10153.correction: Discuss the size of a substance’s specific heat capacity in terms of how hard it is to heat up a certain mass of the substance and how much energy needs to be transferred to heat it up.

10103.belief: A systematic error can be spotted by taking repeat readings.
10103.statement: A systematic error can be spotted by taking repeat readings.
10103.correction: Discuss why the heating of the beaker when measuring specific heat capacity of water will always increase energy measured by the same proportion.

4708.belief: The molecules of a substance change when a substance melts or break down into individual atoms when it boils.
4708.statement: The molecules of a substance change when a substance melts or break down into individual atoms when it boils.
4708.correction: Provide opportunity for pupils to describe, in their own words, the effect on particles of the melting and boiling processes.

10170.belief: The temperature of ice is always 0ºC and the temperature of water in the liquid state cannot be 0°C.
10170.statement: The temperature of ice is always 0ºC and the temperature of water in the liquid state cannot be 0°C.
10170.correction: Make explicit observations that water can be in either or both of the solid and liquid states at 0°C.

10183.belief: The terms current, voltage, resistance, energy and power, together with the properties of each, are often mixed up.
10183.statement: The terms current, voltage, resistance, energy and power, together with the properties of each, are often mixed up.
10183.correction: As each term is introduced during this lesson, spend a few moments checking pupils’ understanding.

3366.belief: The gradient of an I–V graph is equal to 1/R because I = V ÷ R.
3366.statement: The gradient of an I–V graph is equal to 1/R because I = V ÷ R.
3366.correction: Explain how the equation for a straight line graph y = mx + c does not apply in this case because the graph is not a straight line.

6178.statement: Pupils often cannot apply the main I–V graphs to similar components.
6178.correction: Describe how the p.d. and current in components behaves to draw out similarities that can be used to describe unfamiliar components.

561.belief: A battery pushes a constant current around a circuit.
561.statement: A battery pushes a constant current around a circuit.
561.correction: Provide opportunity for pupils to measure p.d. across a power supply when the resistance of a circuit it is connected to is altered.

1666.belief: Circuits are analysed sequentially, starting at the battery and working round, one component at a time.
1666.statement: Circuits are analysed sequentially, starting at the battery and working round, one component at a time.
1666.correction: Ask questions that prompt pupils to consider the effect of changes to one component on the whole circuit.

10419.belief: Travelling at exceptionally high speed through a speed camera means that it will not be able to measure your speed accurately and so it will not trigger.
10419.statement: Travelling at exceptionally high speed through a speed camera means that it will not be able to measure your speed accurately and so it will not trigger.
10419.correction: Tell pupils that speed cameras use radio waves which travel at 300 000 000 m/s. They can accurately measure the speed of objects travelling at thousands of metres per second.

9445.belief: Sound waves somehow “are” the sounds you hear.
9445.statement: Sound waves somehow “are” the sounds you hear.
9445.correction: The sensation of hearing sound (what you hear) is a different thing to what a sound wave is (longitudinal oscillations of particles).

4445.belief: Many students think the mantle is liquid or semi-liquid. Some think it contains soil or water.
4445.statement: Many students think the mantle is liquid or semi-liquid. Some think it contains soil or water.
4445.correction: The mantle is almost all solid rock. Less than 1% of it is liquid e.g. at spreading plate boundaries, subduction zones and hot-spots.

7799.belief: Electric field lines show the movement of moving charges, rather than the force acting on them.
7799.statement: Pupils think that electric field lines show the movement of moving charges, rather than the force acting on them.
7799.correction: Add force arrows to electric field diagrams to show the size of the force they represent at different points.

7164.statement: Pupils may regard force as a property of an object, expressing ideas such as ‘the object has a force’ and ‘the object runs out of force’.
7164.correction: Describe forces as interactions between two objects, using the phrasing ‘the force of object A on object B’.

1781.belief: A common belief is that a resultant force is needed to keep an object in motion, and if no resultant force acts on an object then it must be stationary.
1781.statement: A common belief is that a resultant force is needed to keep an object in motion, and if no resultant force acts on an object then it must be stationary.
1781.correction: Discuss examples in which friction is very low or absent, such as a puck sliding across an ice rink or an object being dropped during a space walk and extrapolate to what would happen if friction disappeared entirely.

1811.belief: It is common for pupils to fail to consider the hanging mass as part of the accelerating mass.
1811.statement: It is common for pupils to fail to consider the hanging mass as part of the accelerating mass.
1811.correction: Emphasise that all of the moving parts in the investigation are connected, are accelerated together, and need to be included in the measurement of the mass being accelerated.

346.belief: When applying the equation F = m × a, pupils may take F to be any one of the forces acting on the object, rather than specifically the resultant force.
346.statement: When applying the equation F = m × a, pupils may take F to be any one of the forces acting on the object, rather than specifically the resultant force.
346.correction: Provide some more complex examples, in which forces act in opposite directions, so pupils are required to work out the resultant force in preparation for completing calculations.

6038.belief: As air resistance increases, a falling object decelerates (slows down).
6038.statement: Pupils may believe that as air resistance increases, a falling object decelerates (slows down).
6038.correction: Analyse footage of a falling object played back in slow motion, or frame–by–frame, to show that the speed of a falling object increases, up to a maximum speed, and at no time does it slow down.

6700.statement: Pupils often forget to include thinking distance in the overall stopping distance, or imagine that thinking distance is too short to matter.
6700.correction: Model a situation in which a child steps out from behind a parked car 10 m in front of a driver. At 20 mph the thinking distance is about 6 m and braking distance 6 m; at 30 mph these are 9 m and 14 m.

490.belief: Atoms are visible under powerful optical microscopes.
490.statement: Atoms are visible under powerful optical microscopes.
490.correction: Emphasise that atoms are far too small to see and our descriptions of atoms are models, based on evidence, that help us understand how they behave.

4439.belief: Many pupils are uncertain about the forces attracting or repelling particles inside an atom.
4439.statement: Many pupils are uncertain about the forces attracting or repelling particles inside an atom.
4439.correction: Extend explanations to include electrostatic forces between protons in the nucleus and introduce the strong nuclear force to explain why nuclei do not self destruct.

6194.statement: Pupils may not have a clear understanding of the forces acting between neutrons and protons in an atomic nucleus.
6194.correction: In simple terms, explain the reasons why some nuclei are unstable in terms of electrostatic repulsion, and include ideas about the strong nuclear force attracting protons and neutrons to each other.

224.belief: Alpha and beta particles and gamma radiation are radioactive.
224.statement: Alpha and beta particles and gamma radiation are radioactive.
224.correction: Differentiate between radioactive particles that can emit radiation and the radiation itself. Radiation consists of fast moving particles or radiation that can cause ionisation because their electric fields interact with those of outer electrons.

6364.belief: Most pupils have difficulty in truly understanding randomness.
6364.statement: Most pupils have difficulty in truly understanding randomness.

3664.belief: It is impossible to predict outcomes for random events such as radioactive decay.
3664.statement: It is impossible to predict outcomes for random events such as radioactive decay.
3664.correction: Use analogies to show that random nuclear decay can lead to predictable outcomes, such as the randomness in the order popcorn kernels pop, but the predictability of how quickly all the popcorn takes to cook.

4484.belief: A material exposed to radiation will become radioactive.
4484.statement: A material exposed to radiation will become radioactive.
4484.correction: Take time to clearly distinguish between radioactive contamination and irradiation.

2369.belief: Digital ammeters are always accurate to the smallest amount they display.
2369.statement: Digital ammeters are always accurate to the smallest amount they display.
2369.correction: Show pupils a copy of the specifications of the ammeters they are using that show how accurate they really are.

6515.statement: Pupils find it challenging to think about how current flows through the connections and around the coil in the motor.
6515.correction: Take pupils step–by–step through the building of a motor from a motor kit and provide an opportunity for pupils to build their own working motor to help them to consolidate their understanding.

7971.belief: Light rays are actual physical things that are the constituents of light.
7971.statement: Pupils often think that light rays are actual physical things that are the constituents of light.
7971.correction: It needs to be made explicit through teaching that light rays are imaginary lines that show the direction in which light is travelling.

7191.statement: Pupils sometimes rote-learn what specific examples of refraction look like, rather than developing a more general understanding of the direction waves turn based on changes in wave speed.
7191.correction: Teach pupils the general theory of refraction and apply it to a variety of different examples where wave speed changes (e.g. sound waves refract in the opposite direction to light at an air-glass boundary due to the different wave speeds).

2354.belief: The different 'kinds' of EM radiation are different phenomena to each other and to visible light. Pupils may also think all radiation is dangerous, none is natural and that light is not radiation.
2354.statement: The different 'kinds' of EM radiation are different phenomena to each other and to visible light. Pupils may also think all radiation is dangerous, none is natural and that light is not radiation.
2354.correction: Each 'kind' of EM radiation is the same phenomena as light (i.e. waves/ripples in electric and magnetic fields) just with different frequencies and wavelengths. Try to refer to different frequencies/frequency ranges rather than different 'kinds'.

3790.belief: Infrared radiation is visible and is seen when objects glow.
3790.statement: Infrared radiation is visible and is seen when objects glow.
3790.correction: Distinguish clearly between light radiation and infrared radiation in terms of what is visible and what is not visible.

10995.belief: White surfaces are always poor absorbers of visible light so they must also always be poor absorbers and emitters of infrared.
10995.statement: White surfaces are always poor absorbers of visible light so they must also always be poor absorbers and emitters of infrared.
10995.correction: White paint is a good absorber and emitter of IR. Colour is not always a good guide to effectiveness at emitting/absorbing IR, except for dark+dull surfaces usually being good emitters/absorbers and shiny metal surfaces being poor emitters/absorbers.

3210.belief: Gamma rays are always higher energy (or power), or more dangerous, than other frequencies of EM radiation.
3210.statement: Gamma rays are always higher energy (or power), or more dangerous, than other frequencies of EM radiation.
3210.correction: EM waves transfer their energy in 'chunks' or 'packets'. The energy transferred by one 'packet' of radiation (and so its ionising ability) does depend on frequency. But the power of a beam of radiation depends on the intensity of the radiation too.

4363.belief: The majority of pupils struggle to differentiate between ionising and non–ionising radiation.
4363.statement: The majority of pupils struggle to differentiate between ionising and non–ionising radiation.
4363.correction: Explicitly teach that non–ionising radiation is not able to force electrons off atoms – it cannot turn atoms into ions. What it may be able to do is cause heating by increasing the movement of particles and therefore temperature of the substance.

4358.belief: Mains appliances draw all their electricity from the live wire, without need for a complete circuit.
4358.statement: Mains appliances draw all their electricity from the live wire, without need for a complete circuit.
4358.correction: Show pupils live and neutral wires connected to a AC connections on a power pack (you can use individual wires taken from mains cables) to show complete circuits are necessary, and that mains cables contain these wires.

9263.belief: A short circuit is a circuit that doesn’t work.
9263.statement: A short circuit is a circuit that doesn’t work.
9263.correction: Demonstrate several short circuits and provide opportunity for pupils to describe what they are in their own words.

8595.statement: Pupils often use the terms power and energy interchangeably.
8595.correction: Use concrete examples to show pupils that a greater power transfers energy more quickly.

10535.belief: Understanding electrical circuits is about memorising equations and procedures.
10535.statement: Understanding electrical circuits is about memorising equations and procedures.
10535.correction: Give pupils the opportunity to discuss what happens in a circuit before they attempt to answer questions about it.

10890.belief: The voltage (drop) across power lines is the same as the voltage they transmit.
10890.statement: The voltage (drop) across power lines is the same as the voltage they transmit.
10890.correction: Spend time to clarify that the power transmitted depends on the p.d. between the live and neutral wires, and power dissipated depends on the drop in voltage from one end of a live wire to the other.

8882.belief: Renewable energy resources are more expensive than fossil fuels and cannot meet the demand for electricity on their own.
8882.statement: Renewable energy resources are more expensive than fossil fuels and cannot meet the demand for electricity on their own.
8882.correction: Compare the cost of renewable energy resources with that of fossil fuels and explore advantages in energy storage technologies.

10797.belief: The velocity of an object must be in the same direction as the resultant force acting on the object.
10797.statement: The velocity of an object must be in the same direction as the resultant force acting on the object.
10797.correction: Invite pupils to consider situations in which the resultant force is not in the same direction as the velocity, such as an object that has been thrown upwards and is slowing down as its height increases.

5972.belief: Being able to complete calculations by substituting numbers into an equation is the same as fully understanding the relationship.
5972.statement: Pupils may assume that being able to complete calculations by substituting numbers into an equation is the same as fully understanding the relationship.
5972.correction: Include questions for which pupils are required to explain their understanding.

1702.belief: It is not clear how the magnetic field around a conducting wire interacts with a uniform magnetic field.
1702.statement: It is not clear how the magnetic field around a conducting wire interacts with a uniform magnetic field.
1702.correction: Focus on observing and predicting the direction that a conducting wire is forced in by a uniform magnetic field, and openly admit that explaining this in terms of how the magnetic field interact is too challenging to include in the syllabus.

6280.statement: Pupils often confuse the terms force and momentum.
6280.correction: Make explicit the understanding that forces change the motion of an object, and that the motion of an object (that a force can change) can be described by its momentum.

8489.statement: Pupils often do not understand clearly what is meant by stopping time and cannot explain why longer stopping times result in smaller forces.
8489.correction: Describe stopping time as the time it takes to stop ‘during which a force is acting’, and provide examples of smaller forces stopping moving objects over longer periods of time than larger forces.

7965.belief: A lever gives you ‘something for nothing’ when used as a force multiplier.
7965.statement: Pupils may think that a lever gives you ‘something for nothing’ when used as a force multiplier.
7965.correction: Ask a pupil to lift an object by a particular height (say 10 cm) without a pivot, then with a pivot and a plank as a lever to compare the effort and distance moved in each case.

2420.belief: The distance to a pivot is always the distance along the lever, no matter which direction the force is acting in.
2420.statement: The distance to a pivot is always the distance along the lever, no matter which direction the force is acting in.
2420.correction: Opening a door by pushing on the handle in different directions shows it is harder to open when the shoulder of the person pushing is closer to the pivot (smaller perpendicular distance between the force and the pivot).

8742.belief: Radioactive isotopes disappear when they decay, so that in one half-life half the mass is lost.
8742.statement: Radioactive isotopes disappear when they decay, so that in one half-life half the mass is lost.
8742.correction: Emphasise that the mass of the nuclei at the end of a nuclear fission or fusion are almost identical to the masses of those at the start. There is a very small difference, with mass being converted to energy according to E = mc².

5973.belief: The colours of light will mix in the same way that paints mix.
5973.statement: Pupils assume that the colours of light will mix in the same way that paints mix.
5973.correction: Make it explicit in your teaching that the primary colours of light (red, green and blue) are different, and mix differently, to the primary colours of paint that pupils may have been taught elsewhere (e.g. red, yellow and blue).

8080.belief: There is only one ray of light for each point of light on the image.
8080.statement: Pupils often think there is only one ray of light for each point of light on the image.
8080.correction: Many rays of light pass through the lens from each point on the object, but all the rays from a single point arrive at a single point at the image distance. The rays from each point on the object arrive at corresponding points at the same distance.

2086.belief: Covering over half of a lens will block out rays of light from half the object and the image will appear cut in half.
2086.statement: Covering over half of a lens will block out rays of light from half the object and the image will appear cut in half.
2086.correction: Talk about many rays of light passing through the lens from each point of the object and show pupils that blocking half the lens keeps the same image, only less bright.

8780.belief: Real images always or only form on screens, or a screen is necessary to observe a real image.
8780.statement: Real images always or only form on screens, or a screen is necessary to observe a real image.
8780.correction: Be clear that real images can form on screens, but can also be observed without a screen. Demonstrate looking through a convex lens (e.g. a magnifying glass) at a diminished, inverted real image of a distant object.

3388.belief: Gravity only acts close to the surface of a planet.
3388.statement: Gravity only acts close to the surface of a planet.
3388.correction: Provide examples of motions caused by gravitational forces acting over huge distances of space, such as the orbits of planets.

4727.belief: Motion is always in the direction of the force acting on an object.
4727.statement: Motion is always in the direction of the force acting on an object.
4727.correction: Provide pupils with opportunity to experience a radial force changing the direction of a small object in order to make it move in a circular path.

9591.belief: Stars just exist and do not change over time.
9591.statement: Stars just exist and do not change over time.
9591.correction: Explain the cause and effect of changes in stars and support pupils in explaining these ideas in their own words.

9593.correction: Explore the ideas that Earth’s atmosphere is made of moving air that refracts light from stars in changing directions to distort the light coming from stars.

652.belief: The Big Bang was an explosion in which existing matter blew up.
652.statement: The Big Bang was an explosion in which existing matter blew up.
652.correction: Describe the Big Bang as an expansion of space combined with the creation of all matter in the universe.

5008.belief: Nuclear power stations can explode in a similar way to nuclear bombs.
5008.statement: Nuclear power stations can explode in a similar way to nuclear bombs.
5008.correction: Explain how the fuel in power stations is not sufficiently concentrated to cause nuclear explosions, and the control rods stop them overheating which could cause a conventional explosion that releases contaminants (as happened at Chernobyl).

5007.belief: Nuclear power stations continually emit radiation into the environment.
5007.statement: Nuclear power stations continually emit radiation into the environment.
5007.correction: Clearly distinguish day–to–day processes and the lack of emissions from the generation of nuclear waste, and methods for dealing with it.

4347.belief: Magnets can attract or repel electric charges in a wire.
4347.statement: Magnets can attract or repel electric charges in a wire.
4347.correction: Explain that the correct explanation for what is happening is usually taught to pupils studying physics at university. At this point, it is sufficient to be able to describe and predict what happens when a conductor is moving in a magnetic field.

1812.belief: It is common for pupils to hold the misunderstanding that stationary magnetic fields can attract or repel electric charge or to conflate magnetic and electrostatic effects.
1812.statement: It is common for pupils to hold the misunderstanding that stationary magnetic fields can attract or repel electric charge or to conflate magnetic and electrostatic effects.
1812.correction: Provide opportunities for pupils to explain applications of the motor effect and the generator effect in order to consolidate a scientific understanding.

9353.belief: The size of the current in the primary coil controls the size of current in the secondary coil.
9353.statement: The size of the current in the primary coil controls the size of current in the secondary coil.
9353.correction: Explain how the p.d. across and resistance of the secondary circuit determines the secondary p.d. and therefore current, and how the current adjusts to ensure that the power input is equal to the power output.
